answers_to_analysis_questions.knowledge_approval: Require an explicit knowledge approval workflow. An authorized upload becoming successfully indexed must NOT automatically make the document eligible for RAG retrieval.  **Approval Authority:** - Tenant Admin is responsible for approving or rejecting knowledge documents within their own tenant. - Platform Admin has platform-level oversight but is not the default content approver. - Support Manager and Support Agent have read-only access to approved knowledge. - Approval decisions must be enforced through backend authorization.  **Approval Workflow:** 1. Authorized user uploads a document. 2. The system validates, extracts, chunks, and processes the document. 3. The document is indexed in a non-retrievable state. 4. Its approval status becomes Pending Approval. 5. Tenant Admin reviews the document and explicitly approves or rejects it. 6. Only an approved document version becomes eligible for authorized RAG retrieval. 7. Rejected, pending, failed, or unapproved documents must never appear in search results or AI context.  **Approval States:** - Pending Approval - Approved - Rejected  Maintain processing status separately from approval status.  **Update and Reprocessing Rules:** - Every new document version requires fresh approval. - Any document reprocessing that changes its content, chunks, or embeddings requires re-approval. - On update or reprocessing, invalidate the previous searchable index entries and prevent stale content from being retrieved. - The new version must remain unavailable to RAG until explicitly approved. - Rejected documents must remain unavailable for retrieval until corrected, reprocessed, and approved.  **Audit Requirements:** Record the document ID, version, tenant ID, approver, approval/rejection decision, timestamp, and optional rejection reason. Maintain approval history for audit purposes.  Approval must apply to a specific document version, not merely to the document record.  These rules apply to the first demonstrable release and ensure that RAG uses only explicitly approved, tenant-authorized knowledge.
answers_to_analysis_questions.rbac_matrix: **RBAC Model and Administrative Security Rules**  Implement a centralized, resource/action-based RBAC model for the four predefined roles: Platform Admin, Tenant Admin, Support Manager, and Support Agent.  Do not introduce arbitrary custom roles or tenant-specific permission overrides in the first release.  ### 1. Initial Role and Permission Matrix  **Platform Admin** - Manage tenant provisioning, activation, and deactivation. - Manage platform-level users and provision Tenant Admin accounts. - Manage predefined role-to-permission mappings, subject to administrative safeguards. - Manage global operational settings and retention policies. - Access platform-level audit and operational information. - Perform authorized platform administration without unrestricted routine access to tenant business content. - No self-elevation or self-approval of privileged permission changes.  **Tenant Admin** - Manage users within their own tenant, including creation, editing, activation, and deactivation. - Assign and change predefined roles within their own tenant, excluding Platform Admin. - View the permission matrix without modifying global permission definitions. - View global operational and retention settings. - Upload, update, reprocess, approve, reject, and delete knowledge documents within their own tenant. - Create, view, and edit tickets within their tenant. - View all tickets belonging to their tenant. - Change ticket category and priority. - Perform ticket status actions only through explicitly authorized workflow transitions. - View tenant-level ticket analytics and authorized audit information. - Cannot provision or access other tenants or modify global RBAC and retention policies.  **Support Manager** - View tickets belonging to their assigned support team. - Create and edit authorized team tickets. - Assign and reassign tickets to eligible members of their assigned team. - Change authorized ticket status, category, and priority. - Escalate team tickets. - View team-level ticket history, activity, and analytics. - View authorized customer and knowledge information. - Cannot manage tenants, users, global RBAC, or global operational settings. - Cannot access tickets belonging to other teams unless explicitly authorized.  **Support Agent** - Create new tickets. - View and edit tickets assigned to them or otherwise explicitly permitted. - Update authorized ticket fields and perform permitted status transitions. - Suggest or override AI-generated category and priority values within their permissions. - Request ticket escalation. - Search approved knowledge documents. - Use authorized customer lookup and AI assistance tools. - View their own permitted activity. - Cannot assign or reassign tickets, manage users, modify permissions, or access unauthorized team/tenant data.  ### 2. Resource/Action Authorization  Implement explicit permissions using resource/action pairs, including:  - Tenant: Create, Read, Update, Activate, Deactivate. - User: Create, Read, Update, Activate, Deactivate. - Role: Read, Assign. - Permission Matrix: Read, Update. - Operational Settings: Read, Update. - Retention Policies: Read, Update. - Knowledge Documents: Create, Read, Update, Approve, Reject, Reprocess, Delete. - Tickets: Create, Read, Update, Assign, Reassign, Escalate, ChangeStatus, ChangePriority, ChangeCategory. - Teams: Read, ManageMembership, AssignTickets. - Analytics: ReadTenant, ReadTeam, ReadOwn. - Audit: ReadPlatform, ReadTenant, ReadTeam, ReadOwn.  Each permission must be explicitly mapped to an authorized role and enforced by the backend. An unlisted or undefined permission must be denied by default.  ### 3. Platform Admin Privilege and Self-Elevation Safeguards  - Platform Admin must not be able to directly increase their own privileges or assign themselves additional roles. - Changes affecting Platform Admin permissions or privileged platform access require approval from a second independent authorized Platform Admin. - The initiating administrator cannot approve their own change. - If a second authorized Platform Admin is unavailable, keep the change pending until independent approval is available. - Prevent modification or deletion of immutable security controls and protected audit records. - Record the initiator, approver, before/after permission values, timestamp, and reason for each privileged change. - Enforce authorization and approval checks server-side. - Prevent privilege escalation through API manipulation, role assignment, or configuration changes. - Tenant Admin must never assign Platform Admin privileges. - Provide controlled bootstrap provisioning for the initial Platform Admin without introducing a self-service privilege escalation mechanism.  ### 4. Permission Configuration and Audit  - Maintain a centralized permission catalogue and versioned role-to-permission mappings. - Allow Platform Admin to manage approved permission mappings subject to safeguards. - Allow Tenant Admin to view but not modify global permission definitions. - Audit every role assignment, permission change, and privileged administrative action. - Apply permission changes consistently across API endpoints and frontend functionality. - Ensure permission revocation takes effect for subsequent authorization checks.  ### 5. Team-Level Access Boundary  Support Manager access must be restricted to explicitly assigned support teams.  The support-team entity, team creation authority, team membership management, and exact ticket visibility rules will be finalized through the separate Support Team decision.  Ticket status transitions and additional Tenant Admin ticket actions will follow the separately agreed ticket workflow decision.  **Security Acceptance Criteria:**  - No unauthorized cross-tenant access. - No unauthorized cross-team ticket access. - No self-elevation or self-approval of privileged changes. - No Tenant Admin assignment of Platform Admin privileges. - No unauthorized modification of protected RBAC configuration or audit records. - All denied authorization attempts must be handled safely and appropriately logged.  These rules define the proposed first-release RBAC and security model. Detailed team ownership and ticket transition permissions remain subject to their respective decision gates.
answers_to_analysis_questions.support_teams: **Support Team Creation and Membership Management**  Implement tenant-scoped support team management as part of the Administrative Console.  ### 1. Team Creation and Ownership - Tenant Admin can create, view, edit, activate, and deactivate support teams within their own tenant. - Each team belongs to exactly one tenant. - Platform Admin has platform-level oversight but does not routinely manage tenant team membership. - Support Manager and Support Agent cannot create or modify team structures.  ### 2. Team Membership Management - Tenant Admin manages team membership within their tenant. - Tenant Admin assigns one primary Support Manager to each team. - A Support Manager may be responsible for one or more teams. - Each Support Agent belongs to exactly one primary support team in the first release. - Tenant Admin can add or remove eligible Support Agents and change team membership. - Support Manager can view their assigned team's membership but cannot add, remove, or change members. - Membership changes must be authorized, tenant-scoped, and audit logged.  ### 3. Support Manager Ticket Visibility  **Team-assigned tickets:** - Support Manager can view all tickets assigned to their explicitly assigned teams, regardless of which team member is the individual ticket assignee. - Support Manager can view ticket details, status, category, priority, assignment, and authorized activity history.  **Unassigned tickets within an assigned team:** - Support Manager can view all tickets assigned to their team's queue but not yet assigned to an individual agent. - Support Manager can assign or reassign these tickets to eligible agents within their assigned teams. - These tickets must be included in team-level workload and operational views.  **Tickets belonging to other teams:** - Support Manager cannot view or modify tickets belonging to teams they are not assigned to manage. - Cross-team access requires an explicit separately authorized administrative permission; it must not be granted implicitly.  **Completely unassigned tickets:** - Tickets without an assigned team or individual agent are visible to Tenant Admin and an authorized central triage function. - Tenant Admin or authorized triage personnel can route these tickets to the appropriate support team. - Support Managers cannot access globally unassigned tickets outside their assigned teams.  ### 4. Ticket Assignment Rules - Maintain separate AssignedTeamId and AssignedAgentId relationships. - A ticket may be assigned to a team while remaining unassigned to an individual agent. - An individual agent can only be assigned tickets belonging to their authorized team, unless an explicitly approved exception exists. - Support Manager can assign and reassign tickets only within their assigned teams. - Tenant Admin can perform authorized tenant-level ticket routing and oversight. - All assignment and reassignment operations must validate team membership and tenant ownership on the backend.  ### 5. Security and Audit Requirements - Enforce tenant isolation and team-level authorization on every ticket API and data access path. - Prevent unauthorized cross-team ticket visibility. - Revalidate team membership and authorization when accessing or modifying tickets. - Record team creation, updates, activation/deactivation, membership changes, manager assignments, ticket assignments, and reassignments in the audit trail. - Team deactivation must not silently delete historical tickets or audit records. Existing assignments must be reviewed and safely reassigned.  These rules apply to the first demonstrable release. Multi-team membership for individual agents and dynamic team hierarchies are deferred for future consideration.
answers_to_analysis_questions.ticket_workflow: **Ticket Lifecycle, Status Transitions and Tenant Admin Permissions**  Implement a controlled, complete ticket lifecycle with server-side role-based transition authorization.  ### 1. Ticket Status Model  Use the following initial ticket statuses:  - New – Ticket has been created. - Open – Ticket is available for handling. - In Progress – An agent is actively working on it. - Pending Customer – Waiting for customer information or response. - Resolved – The issue has been addressed and is awaiting closure. - Closed – Ticket handling is completed.  Treat escalation as a separate workflow flag/attribute rather than a mutually exclusive ticket status. A ticket can remain In Progress or Pending Customer while being marked as Escalated.  ### 2. Permitted Status Transitions  - New → Open: Authorized user. - Open → In Progress: Assigned Agent or Support Manager. - Open → Closed: Support Manager or Tenant Admin, with a mandatory reason. - In Progress → Pending Customer: Assigned Agent or Support Manager. - In Progress → Resolved: Assigned Agent or Support Manager. - In Progress → Open: Assigned Agent or Support Manager, subject to authorization. - Pending Customer → In Progress: Assigned Agent or Support Manager. - Pending Customer → Resolved: Assigned Agent or Support Manager. - Resolved → Closed: Support Manager or Tenant Admin. - Resolved → Open (Reopen): Support Manager or Tenant Admin, with a mandatory reason. - Closed → Open (Reopen): Support Manager or Tenant Admin, with a mandatory reason.  Reject all undefined transitions by default. Enforce transition rules through backend authorization and workflow validation, not just frontend controls.  ### 3. Resolve, Close and Reopen Rules  **Resolve:** - Assigned Support Agent can resolve their permitted tickets. - Support Manager can resolve tickets belonging to their assigned teams. - Tenant Admin can resolve tickets belonging to their tenant. - Require a resolution summary or resolution notes before resolution. - AI-generated resolution suggestions must never automatically resolve a ticket.  **Close:** - Support Manager can close resolved tickets within their assigned teams. - Tenant Admin can close resolved tickets within their tenant. - Require a valid resolution summary before closure. - Closed tickets become read-only for normal Support Agent operations.  **Reopen:** - Support Manager and Tenant Admin can reopen resolved or closed tickets. - Require a mandatory reopening reason. - Preserve the original resolution, closure details, and complete historical activity. - Allow authorized reassignment after reopening. - Reopening must create a new audit event rather than overwrite previous history.  ### 4. Escalation Rules  - Support Agent can request escalation for an authorized ticket. - Support Manager can escalate tickets belonging to their assigned teams. - Support Manager can specify the escalation reason and adjust priority within authorized limits. - Authorized Support Managers can route escalated tickets to appropriate teams or higher-level support queues. - Escalation must preserve the ticket's underlying workflow status. - Record the escalation initiator, reason, timestamp, previous assignment, and new assignment. - AI may recommend escalation but cannot execute it autonomously.  ### 5. Tenant Admin – Additional Ticket Management Authority  Tenant Admin must have administrative ticket management authority across their own tenant, beyond read-only visibility and oversight.  Allow Tenant Admin to:  - View all tickets belonging to their tenant. - Create and edit tenant tickets. - Update ticket descriptions and permitted metadata. - Change ticket category and priority. - Assign and reassign tickets across support teams within their tenant. - Assign and reassign agents within authorized team membership. - Perform permitted status transitions. - Resolve and close tickets. - Reopen resolved or closed tickets with a mandatory reason. - Escalate tickets and manage tenant-level routing. - View complete ticket history and authorized audit information. - View tenant-level ticket analytics.  Tenant Admin must not access or modify tickets belonging to another tenant.  ### 6. Ticket Deletion and Historical Records  - Do not provide permanent ticket deletion to Tenant Admin, Support Manager, or Support Agent in the first release. - Use controlled closure or cancellation instead of physical deletion. - Preserve ticket history and audit records according to the separately configured retention and deletion policy. - Any future administrative deletion capability must follow an explicit authorization and audited deletion workflow.  ### 7. Audit and Security Requirements  Record all important ticket operations, including:  - Ticket creation and editing. - Status changes and transition reasons. - Resolution and closure details. - Reopening reasons. - Escalation events. - Priority and category changes. - Team and agent assignments/reassignments. - Actor identity, tenant, timestamp, and before/after values.  Apply tenant isolation, team-level authorization, and role-based transition guards on every relevant API endpoint.  Platform Admin should have operational oversight and audited, minimized access. Routine Platform Admin operations must not bypass tenant business authorization.  ### 8. Acceptance Criteria  - Only authorized roles can execute permitted ticket transitions. - Invalid transitions are rejected by the backend. - Resolution and closure require the appropriate mandatory information. - Reopening preserves historical records. - Escalation does not destroy the underlying ticket workflow status. - Tenant Admin can perform authorized administrative ticket operations across their own tenant. - Support Manager remains restricted to assigned teams. - Support Agent remains restricted to permitted tickets and actions. - No unauthorized cross-tenant or cross-team access is possible. - All material ticket operations are auditable.  These rules define the proposed first-release ticket workflow. Advanced workflow customization, automatic escalation, external ticketing integrations, and permanent deletion workflows can be considered separately.
answers_to_analysis_questions.customer_lookup: **Role-Based Customer and Related Ticket Lookup Fields**  Implement a read-only, allowlisted Customer Lookup and Related Ticket Lookup tool for the first release. Apply strict tenant, role, team, and ticket-level authorization before returning any customer or ticket information.  ### 1. Permitted Customer Fields  Allow the following minimum customer fields, where available:  - Customer ID. - Customer Display Name. - Company / Organization Name. - Customer Account Status. - Customer Created Date. - Email Address (masked by default).  Do not expose phone numbers, physical addresses, payment/financial details, passwords, authentication credentials, or other unnecessary sensitive customer information through the first-release lookup tool.  ### 2. Permitted Related Ticket Fields  Allow the following fields according to the requesting user's authorization:  - Ticket ID. - Ticket Subject. - Ticket Description (only for tickets the user is authorized to access). - Ticket Status. - Category. - Priority. - Assigned Team. - Assigned Agent. - Created Date. - Last Updated Date. - Escalation Status. - Resolution Summary, subject to ticket access permissions.  Do not expose internal notes, confidential staff discussions, unrestricted conversation history, or attachments through this customer lookup tool in the first release.  ### 3. Role-Based Access  **Platform Admin:** - No routine unrestricted customer business-data lookup. - Access to customer information is restricted to separately authorized, audited platform investigation requirements. - No implicit access to all tenant customer records through the lookup tool.  **Tenant Admin:** - Can search and view customer information within their own tenant. - Can view all related tickets belonging to their own tenant. - Can view authorized customer and ticket fields. - Cannot access other tenants' customer or ticket information.  **Support Manager:** - Can search and view customers associated with tickets belonging to their explicitly assigned support teams. - Can view related team tickets, including tickets assigned to the team but not yet assigned to an individual agent. - Cannot access customers or tickets belonging exclusively to other teams. - Cannot access globally unassigned tickets unless separately authorized for central triage.  **Support Agent:** - Can search and view customers associated with tickets assigned to them or otherwise explicitly permitted. - Can view authorized customer details and related permitted tickets. - Cannot browse unrestricted tenant-wide customer records or access another team's restricted customer information.  ### 4. Privacy and Data Minimization  - Mask customer email addresses by default. - Exclude phone numbers, physical addresses, financial/payment details, and authentication information from the first-release tool. - Exclude internal notes and confidential staff-only content. - Return only fields necessary for the requested support operation. - Do not include unnecessary personal data in AI prompts, tool responses, application logs, or audit records.  ### 5. Read-Only Tool Restrictions  The customer and ticket lookup tools must be strictly read-only.  - No customer creation, editing, deletion, or modification. - No ticket creation, editing, assignment, reassignment, status change, or deletion through these lookup tools. - Business-data changes must use separate authorized application workflows with explicit human action and appropriate permission checks. - AI must never use lookup access to bypass RBAC or tenant restrictions.  ### 6. Authorization and Audit Requirements  - Enforce tenant and role authorization on the backend for every lookup request. - Apply team-level and ticket-level access filters before retrieving or returning data. - Validate all customer and ticket identifiers against the authenticated user's authorized tenant and access scope. - Prevent direct-ID enumeration and unauthorized cross-tenant or cross-team lookups. - Use typed, validated request and response schemas. - Record tool name, actor, tenant, access outcome, timestamp, and correlation ID in the audit trail. - Avoid logging unnecessary customer content or sensitive personal data.  ### 7. Acceptance Criteria  - Each role receives only its explicitly permitted customer and ticket fields. - Support Manager cannot retrieve another team's restricted customer information. - Support Agent cannot retrieve unrelated tenant-wide customer records. - Tenant Admin can access authorized customer and ticket information across their own tenant. - Platform Admin has no unrestricted routine customer lookup access. - Unauthorized requests are denied by the backend. - Lookup tools cannot perform write operations. - Internal notes, payment information, authentication details, and unauthorized personal information are never returned.  These restrictions apply to the first demonstrable release. Additional customer profile fields, full conversation history, attachments, and expanded customer data access can be considered separately.
answers_to_analysis_questions.retention_audit: **Centralized Retention, Deletion, Audit and Tenant Lifecycle Policy**  Implement configurable, centralized data retention and deletion management covering tickets, customers, users, feedback, ticket activity, ticket AI results, conversations, application logs, and audit records.  The following are proposed initial retention defaults for the first demonstrable release, not regulatory or legal retention commitments.  ### 1. Initial Retention Periods  | Data Category | Proposed Retention | |---|---| | Active Tickets | While the ticket remains active | | Closed Tickets | 365 days after closure | | Customer Records | While associated active tickets exist; thereafter according to applicable ticket retention | | Inactive Customer Records | 365 days after the last related ticket closure | | Active Users | While the account remains active | | Deactivated User Records | 365 days after deactivation | | User Activity Records | 365 days | | Ticket Activity and History | Retain with the associated ticket, subject to its retention policy | | Customer Feedback | 90 days | | Ticket AI Results | 90 days | | Conversations | 90 days | | Application Logs | 30 days | | Security and Administrative Audit Logs | 365 days | | Evaluation Data and Results | 90 days | | Backups | Maximum 30 days |  Original knowledge documents, versions, extracted content, chunks, and embeddings must follow the previously defined document retention and deletion policies.  Audit records required for security and accountability must have their own retention lifecycle, independent of ordinary business-data deletion.  ### 2. Configurable Retention Management  Provide a dedicated administrative retention and deletion management module.  **Platform Admin:** - View and configure global retention policies. - Configure retention periods for supported data categories. - Enable or disable applicable cleanup policies. - Review policy versions and change history. - Monitor scheduled cleanup operations. - View pending, completed, and failed deletion operations. - Initiate authorized cleanup operations.  **Tenant Admin:** - View applicable retention policies. - Delete authorized knowledge documents and permitted tenant data through approved workflows. - Cannot modify global retention policies.  **Support Manager and Support Agent:** - No retention-policy administration permissions.  Retention policy changes must be validated, versioned, and audit logged.  ### 3. Ticket, Customer and User Data Deletion  **Tickets:** - No permanent ticket deletion by Support Agent, Support Manager, or Tenant Admin in the first release. - Use controlled closure or cancellation instead of physical deletion. - Preserve ticket activity and historical attribution. - Purge eligible ticket data only through the authorized retention process.  **Customer Records:** - Preserve referential integrity between customers and their related tickets. - Do not delete customer records while associated active tickets exist. - Purge or anonymize eligible customer information according to the applicable retention policy. - Do not retain unnecessary personal information.  **User Records:** - Deactivation must immediately revoke authentication and application access. - Preserve historical ticket and audit attribution. - Do not physically delete a user record in a way that breaks historical references. - Apply the approved retention policy before purging personal user information.  ### 4. Audit Logging and Access Permissions  Maintain separate application logs, security audit logs, administrative audit logs, and ticket activity history.  Record relevant events including: - Authentication and access-control events. - User creation, modification, activation, deactivation, and role changes. - Tenant creation, activation, deactivation, and deletion. - RBAC and permission matrix changes. - Retention policy modifications. - Knowledge document upload, approval, rejection, reprocessing, and deletion. - Ticket creation, modification, assignment, status transitions, escalation, resolution, closure, and reopening. - Customer lookup and authorized AI tool execution. - Data deletion and cleanup outcomes.  Each applicable audit record should include actor, tenant, action, resource identifier, timestamp, outcome, and correlation ID.  **Audit Access Matrix:**  - **Platform Admin:** Platform security events, privileged administrative changes, tenant lifecycle events, and platform audit information. - **Tenant Admin:** Audit records relating to their own tenant, including user management, role assignments, knowledge administration, retention-related activity, and ticket operations. - **Support Manager:** Authorized team-level ticket activity and relevant operational events. - **Support Agent:** Their own permitted ticket activity and relevant personal activity records.  Audit records must be protected against unauthorized modification and deletion. Audit-log access must itself be audited.  Do not store passwords, secrets, unnecessary customer content, or sensitive prompt data in audit records.  ### 5. Tenant Deactivation Policy  Tenant deactivation must immediately: - Disable authentication and login for all users belonging to the tenant. - Revoke API, AI tool, and application access. - Prevent tenant data from appearing in RAG retrieval or search results. - Stop new tenant-specific processing and scheduled operations safely. - Preserve existing tickets, customer records, documents, conversations, and audit history. - Retain the data according to the applicable retention policies. - Allow controlled reactivation by an authorized Platform Admin.  Tenant deactivation must NOT automatically delete tenant data.  ### 6. Tenant Deletion Policy  Implement a separate, explicitly authorized tenant deletion workflow.  1. Tenant Admin can submit a tenant deletion request. 2. Platform Admin reviews the request. 3. A second independent authorized Platform Admin must approve permanent deletion. 4. The tenant immediately enters a deactivated / pending-deletion state. 5. Revoke all user, API, AI, search, and application access. 6. Apply a 30-day deletion grace period. 7. Allow an authorized reversal during the grace period, subject to approval. 8. After the grace period and required approval, permanently purge eligible tenant business data and derived data. 9. Verify deletion across Azure SQL, Blob Storage, Azure AI Search indexes, embeddings, conversations, feedback, and related stored artifacts. 10. Allow backup copies to expire within the defined maximum 30-day backup retention period. 11. Preserve only the minimum necessary tenant deletion audit metadata under its independent retention policy.  If independent approval is unavailable, permanent deletion must remain pending and must not be self-approved.  ### 7. Security and Deletion Acceptance Criteria  - Tenant deactivation immediately prevents unauthorized access without deleting retained data. - Tenant deletion requires independent approval. - Deletion must cover primary records, derived data, indexes, and applicable stored artifacts. - Deleted knowledge must become unavailable to RAG immediately. - Historical ticket attribution and required audit records must remain consistent. - Retention policies must be configurable and auditable. - Unauthorized users must not be able to view, modify, or delete protected audit records. - Tenant isolation must be maintained throughout deactivation, deletion, and cleanup. - Failed cleanup operations must be observable and safely retryable.  These retention periods are initial proposed defaults for the demonstrable release and require validation against applicable business, privacy, and legal obligations before production use. The retention policy must remain configurable rather than hardcoded.
answers_to_analysis_questions.timeouts: **API and AI Model Timeout Strategy – Asynchronous Processing**  Adopt asynchronous processing for potentially long-running AI operations rather than forcing all AI model requests to complete within the general 30-second API timeout.  ### 1. General API Timeout  - Maintain a default 30-second timeout for general synchronous API requests. - Simple CRUD operations, authentication, authorization, customer lookup, ticket lookup, and job-status queries should remain synchronous and complete within the normal API timeout. - AI request submission APIs should validate and accept requests quickly without waiting for full model execution.  ### 2. Asynchronous AI Processing  Use a background job architecture for potentially long-running operations, including:  - RAG chat and AI answer generation. - Ticket summarization. - Ticket classification and priority suggestions. - AI-generated reply drafts. - Sentiment and urgency analysis. - Knowledge extraction, chunking, and embedding generation. - Document reprocessing and bulk indexing.  The API should: 1. Validate the request and enforce tenant/role authorization. 2. Create a uniquely identifiable AI job. 3. Persist the job metadata and relevant execution context. 4. Enqueue the job for background processing. 5. Return HTTP 202 Accepted with a Job ID and status endpoint. 6. Process the request through a background worker. 7. Persist the validated result or safe failure information. 8. Make the result available through an authorized status/result API.  ### 3. Job Status Management  Maintain the following job states:  - Queued - Processing - Completed - Failed - Timed Out - Cancelled  The frontend must display the current processing status and retrieve the completed result through an authorized API.  Use lightweight client polling or an appropriate notification mechanism. Status polling must not repeatedly trigger the AI operation.  ### 4. Model Timeout and Retry Configuration  - Configure model-provider timeouts independently from general API timeouts. - Allow longer AI execution within a configurable, bounded background-processing timeout. - Do not artificially reduce model timeouts merely to fit the general 30-second API limit. - Configure timeout values based on operation type, provider constraints, observed latency, and evaluation results. - Implement bounded retries with exponential backoff for eligible transient failures and throttling responses. - Avoid retrying permanent validation, authorization, or invalid-request failures. - Ensure retries are safe and do not create duplicate business records or duplicate jobs. - Record timeout, retry, latency, and failure information with correlation IDs.  ### 5. Security and Reliability  - Persist background job metadata so processing does not depend on in-memory application state. - Maintain tenant ID, requesting user, operation type, and authorization context for every job. - Revalidate access when retrieving job status and results. - Prevent cross-tenant job access and unauthorized result retrieval. - Do not expose secrets, provider stack traces, or sensitive model errors to clients. - Handle worker failures, queue failures, provider throttling, and partial processing safely. - Support safe recovery and retry of eligible failed jobs.  ### 6. Frontend Behaviour  - Return an immediate acknowledgement when an AI request is accepted. - Display queued and processing indicators. - Allow users to continue using other application features while AI processing runs. - Retrieve and display the result when processing completes. - Display a clear, actionable error when processing fails or times out. - Prevent duplicate submissions caused by repeated clicks or network retries.  ### 7. Acceptance Criteria  - General synchronous APIs retain a 30-second default timeout. - Long-running AI operations execute independently in background workers. - AI request submission returns a Job ID and HTTP 202 Accepted. - Client status queries return the correct job state. - Completed AI results are available only to authorized users. - Model timeouts are configurable independently from API timeouts. - Transient failures support bounded and safe retries. - Tenant isolation is enforced across job creation, execution, status, and result retrieval. - Job execution and failures are observable through structured logs and correlation IDs.  This asynchronous architecture applies to the first demonstrable release. Streaming responses, advanced real-time notifications, and distributed job orchestration enhancements can be considered separately if justified.
answers_to_analysis_questions.evaluation_targets: **Evaluation Target Governance, Scoring Methodology and Quality Gates**  ### 1. Evaluation Targets Must Remain Non-Gating  All proposed AI evaluation percentages must remain non-gating evaluation targets after Requirement v1.1 approval.  Approving Requirement v1.1 must not automatically convert proposed grounding, citation, retrieval, abstention, or structured-output percentages into mandatory release gates.  - Evaluation metrics are intended to measure quality, identify weaknesses, and support improvement. - Initial percentage targets must not independently block Requirement Approval or release acceptance. - Mandatory percentage-based quality gates may be introduced only through a separately authorized decision with documented rationale, measurement methodology, representative evaluation data, and acceptance criteria. - Record evaluation results, limitations, and known weaknesses transparently.  This does not make security, authorization, data integrity, or core functional acceptance criteria optional. Those remain mandatory.  ### 2. Grounding Scoring Methodology  Measure grounding at the factual-claim level.  Grounding Score =  Supported factual claims / Total evaluated factual claims × 100.  A factual claim is considered supported only when the approved retrieved evidence directly supports the claim.  - Denominator: All factual claims evaluated in the response. - Numerator: Claims supported by authorized retrieved knowledge. - Unsupported, contradicted, or unverifiable factual claims must not be counted as supported. - Use human-reviewed evaluation labels for the initial baseline. - Responses that correctly abstain when evidence is insufficient must be evaluated separately under abstention quality, not automatically treated as grounding failures.  ### 3. Citation Correctness and Coverage  Measure citation correctness separately from citation coverage.  **Citation Correctness:**  Correct and supporting citations / Total citations emitted × 100.  - Denominator: All citations emitted by the assistant. - Numerator: Citations that resolve to the correct authorized source and genuinely support the associated claim. - Broken, incorrect, irrelevant, or non-supporting citations count as incorrect.  **Citation Coverage:**  Claims with at least one supporting citation / Total claims requiring citations × 100.  - Denominator: All factual claims that require source attribution. - Numerator: Claims with at least one correct supporting citation.  A response with no citations must not receive an artificial 100% citation correctness score. Report the metric as not applicable where there are no emitted citations, and report missing citation coverage separately.  ### 4. Invalid Structured Output Measurement  Measure structured-output validity for ticket summarization, classification, priority, and other schema-based AI operations.  **Initial Invalid Output Rate:**  Invalid first-attempt outputs / Total structured-output attempts × 100.  **Final Unrecoverable Invalid Output Rate:**  Outputs remaining invalid after permitted retries / Total structured-output attempts × 100.  Validate: - JSON syntax. - Required fields. - Field types. - Allowed enum values. - Schema constraints. - Business validation rules.  Invalid model outputs must be rejected or safely retried. They must never corrupt or overwrite persisted ticket data.  Record initial failures and final validation outcomes separately.  ### 5. Evaluation Dataset and Baseline  Use the initial evaluation dataset defined in the PRD:  - At least 50 question/source pairs. - At least 10 no-answer questions. - At least 10 prompt-injection cases.  Also use synthetic ticket scenarios to evaluate ticket summaries, classification, priority suggestions, and structured-output validity.  Each evaluation run must record: - Evaluation dataset version. - Model and deployment identifier. - Prompt version. - Run date and status. - Total evaluated samples. - Metric numerators and denominators. - Individual results and failure cases. - Comparison with the previous baseline. - Known limitations.  Use human-reviewed expected answers, source references, and structured-output expectations wherever applicable.  ### 6. Mandatory Acceptance Criteria Versus Evaluation Targets  The following remain mandatory regardless of evaluation percentages:  - No unauthorized cross-tenant or cross-team data access. - Backend authorization for protected APIs and tools. - No persistence of invalid structured model output. - No fabricated citations or unsupported factual answers presented as grounded. - Safe abstention when evidence is insufficient. - Human review before customer-facing communication or business-changing AI actions. - Proper handling of timeouts, model failures, and unauthorized tool calls. - Auditability of relevant AI operations.  Grounding, citation correctness, retrieval relevance, abstention quality, prompt-injection scores, and structured-output percentages remain non-gating evaluation metrics until separately authorized as formal quality gates.  ### 7. Future Threshold Governance  Defer final numeric evaluation thresholds and release-blocking percentages until representative baseline evaluation results are available.  Before introducing mandatory thresholds, document:  - The metric definition. - Scoring methodology and denominator. - Evaluation dataset and sample size. - Expected threshold and its justification. - Measurement repeatability. - Exception and failure-handling rules. - Approval authority and effective requirement version.  Any future change from a non-gating target to a mandatory release gate requires a separate authorized decision and must not be inferred merely from Requirement v1.1 approval.  This approach preserves measurable AI quality improvement without prematurely imposing unsupported percentage-based release restrictions.
answers_to_analysis_questions.account_recovery: **Local Authentication and Account Recovery – ASP.NET Core Identity**  Use the built-in ASP.NET Core Identity password recovery and account management capabilities for the first release. Do not introduce a custom password-reset token or authentication recovery implementation.  The first demonstrable release should use local authentication with ASP.NET Core Identity, keeping the authentication architecture extensible for a future Microsoft Entra ID integration. Enterprise SSO remains deferred.  ### 1. Password Policy  - Minimum password length: 12 characters. - Use ASP.NET Core Identity password hashing and validation. - Never store passwords in plain text or reversible form. - Passwords must never be visible or retrievable by administrators. - Make password policy configurable. - Provide authenticated users with a secure password-change workflow. - Apply appropriate password reuse and compromised-password protections where supported.  ### 2. Password Reset Token Policy  - Use ASP.NET Core Identity's built-in password-reset token generation and validation. - Deliver reset instructions only to the user's registered email address. - Initial proposed reset-token validity: 30 minutes. - Tokens must be protected, time-limited, and invalidated after successful password reset. - A previously used or expired token must not permit another password reset. - Require HTTPS for all password-reset operations. - Do not expose reset tokens in application logs, telemetry, or audit records. - Invalid or expired tokens must require a fresh reset request.  ### 3. Account Lockout Policy  Use ASP.NET Core Identity's configurable lockout functionality.  Initial proposed configuration: - Maximum 5 consecutive failed login attempts. - Temporary lockout duration of 15 minutes. - Reset or manage failed-attempt counters according to successful authentication and Identity policy. - Apply additional request rate limiting to login and password-reset endpoints. - Prevent permanent account lockout through repeated failed attempts. - Allow authorized administrative unlocking where necessary. - Audit lockout, unlock, and repeated authentication failure events.  These initial values must remain configurable rather than hardcoded.  ### 4. Self-Service Account Recovery Workflow  Implement the following workflow:  1. User selects Forgot Password. 2. User enters their registered email address. 3. The application provides a generic confirmation response without revealing whether the account exists. 4. If an eligible account exists, ASP.NET Core Identity generates a protected password-reset token. 5. Send a time-limited HTTPS password-reset link to the registered email address. 6. User validates the token and submits a new password. 7. Validate the token and new password through ASP.NET Core Identity. 8. Invalidate previous recovery tokens and revoke existing authentication sessions and refresh tokens where applicable. 9. Notify the user that their password has been successfully changed. 10. Require a fresh login using the new password.  ### 5. Account Enumeration and Recovery Security  - Return equivalent responses for existing and non-existing email addresses. - Apply rate limiting to password-reset requests. - Do not disclose account status, lockout details, or sensitive authentication information to unauthorized callers. - Do not log passwords, reset tokens, or complete reset URLs. - Protect reset links against tampering and unauthorized reuse. - Use secure email delivery and avoid exposing tokens to third-party tracking systems. - Record security-relevant recovery events without storing sensitive credentials.  ### 6. Administrative Password Recovery Permissions  **Platform Admin:** - Can perform authorized account recovery support and unlock operations. - Cannot view or retrieve existing passwords. - Cannot bypass password-reset token validation.  **Tenant Admin:** - Can initiate or resend password-reset instructions for users belonging to their own tenant. - Can manage authorized account activation and deactivation. - Cannot view, retrieve, or directly set another user's password. - Cannot reset accounts belonging to another tenant.  **Support Manager and Support Agent:** - No administrative password recovery permissions. - Users can use their own self-service password recovery functionality.  All administrative recovery and account-unlock actions must be audit logged.  ### 7. Account and Tenant Deactivation Interaction  - A deactivated user cannot authenticate, even if they successfully reset their password. - Password reset must never automatically reactivate a deactivated user. - A deactivated tenant must prevent authentication and application access for all its users. - Tenant or user reactivation must require a separate authorized administrative action. - Preserve required historical ticket and audit attribution.  ### 8. Authentication Provider Extensibility  - Keep ASP.NET Core Identity authentication concerns separated from application business logic. - Keep role, tenant, and authorization checks enforced server-side. - Design the authentication boundary so Microsoft Entra ID can be integrated as a future provider. - Do not implement enterprise SSO as a mandatory first-release dependency.  ### 9. Acceptance Criteria  - Users can securely request and complete password resets. - Reset tokens expire after the configured validity period. - Used or expired tokens cannot be reused. - Account enumeration is prevented. - Login lockout and rate limiting operate as configured. - Administrative users cannot view or retrieve passwords. - Tenant Admin recovery actions remain restricted to their own tenant. - Password reset does not reactivate disabled accounts or tenants. - Previous authentication sessions are invalidated following successful password reset, subject to the supported session architecture. - Authentication and recovery events are securely auditable. - All password recovery and authentication endpoints use appropriate HTTPS and server-side security controls.  These requirements apply to the first demonstrable release. MFA, passwordless authentication, advanced recovery methods, and enterprise SSO can be considered separately.

followup_clarifications_and_update_autho.additional_rules:
**Detailed Rules for Ticket Cancellation and Real Email Provider Integration**

### A. Ticket Cancellation ? First Release

Introduce a distinct Cancelled status as a separate terminal ticket outcome.

**Permitted Transitions:**
- New ? Cancelled.
- Open ? Cancelled.
- In Progress ? Cancelled.
- Pending Customer ? Cancelled.

Do not allow:
- Resolved ? Cancelled.
- Closed ? Cancelled.
- Cancelled ? Resolved or Closed.
- Cancelled ? Reopened through the normal workflow.

**Role-Based Permissions:**
1. Tenant Admin: Can cancel any ticket belonging to their own tenant.
2. Support Manager: Can cancel tickets belonging to their assigned support teams, including unassigned tickets within those teams.
3. Support Agent: Can submit a cancellation request for tickets they are authorized to access but cannot finalize cancellation independently.
4. Platform Admin: No routine business-ticket cancellation permission. Exceptional intervention requires explicit authorization and audit logging.

**Mandatory Cancellation Information:**
- Cancellation Reason: Customer Withdrawn, Duplicate Ticket, Created in Error, No Longer Required, or Other.
- Cancellation Notes: Mandatory explanation.
- Cancelled By: Authenticated user ID.
- Cancellation Timestamp.
- Previous Ticket Status.

**Cancellation Behaviour:**
- Cancelled is a terminal status distinct from Resolved and Closed.
- Cancelled tickets must be excluded from successful resolution and closure metrics.
- Preserve ticket details, conversation history, assignment history, and audit records.
- Do not permanently delete cancelled tickets.
- If further support is required, create a new ticket and link it to the original cancelled ticket.
- Enforce all tenant-level and team-level authorization checks on the backend.

### B. Real Email Provider ? First Release

Include one real email delivery provider in the first release to support fully functional password recovery and other approved transactional email notifications.

**Provider Selection:**
- Integrate one provider through SMTP or its supported email delivery API.
- Azure Communication Services Email or SendGrid are acceptable candidates.
- Final provider selection can be made during implementation based on cost, reliability, security, and deployment compatibility.
- Keep provider integration behind a configurable email service abstraction to allow future provider replacement.

**Environment-Specific Delivery:**
1. Development: Real email delivery to controlled developer/test accounts.
2. Testing: Real email delivery to authorized test accounts.
3. Demo: Real email delivery to registered demonstration users.
4. Production: Real email delivery to verified registered users through the configured production provider.

**Email Security and Delivery Controls:**
- Use environment-specific sender identities and provider configurations.
- Store SMTP credentials and API keys in secure secret management, never in source code.
- Verify sender-domain authentication and provider configuration.
- Use HTTPS for password-reset links.
- Send ASP.NET Core Identity password-reset emails using secure, time-limited, single-use tokens.
- Apply rate limiting and abuse protection to email-triggering endpoints.
- Prevent development and testing environments from accidentally sending emails to arbitrary external recipients; use controlled recipient allowlists.
- Do not log passwords, reset tokens, complete reset URLs, or provider secrets.
- Record delivery status, timestamp, message correlation ID, and safe error metadata.
- Implement bounded retries for eligible transient delivery failures.
- Handle permanent delivery failures without exposing sensitive information.
- Do not treat an accepted email request as proof of successful inbox delivery.

**Password Recovery Availability:**
- Self-service password recovery must work end-to-end using actual email delivery.
- If the email provider is unavailable, return a safe error and allow a controlled retry.
- Do not silently mark a password-reset email as delivered when delivery fails.
- Administrative recovery must remain separately authorized and audited.

### C. First-Release Scope

Both the distinct Cancelled ticket status and real email provider integration are included in the first demonstrable release. The email provider is a configurable implementation choice, not a reason to defer real email functionality. All cancellation and email operations must respect RBAC, tenant isolation, and audit requirements.

retention_and_reversal_clarifications.additional_policy_details:
**Additional Conditions for Cancelled Ticket Retention and Tenant Deletion Reversal**

### A. Cancelled Ticket Retention
- Apply the same configurable 365-day retention policy used for closed tickets.
- Start the retention period from the actual ticket cancellation timestamp.
- Treat cancellation as a terminal ticket event for customer retention calculations.
- Retain customer records while any associated tickets remain active or in a non-terminal state.
- Once all associated tickets reach a terminal state (Closed or Cancelled), calculate customer retention from the latest terminal-ticket timestamp.
- Retain the customer record for 365 days after that latest terminal date, subject to applicable legal holds and authorized retention exceptions.
- Preserve required ticket activity and audit records according to their independent retention policies.
- Do not permanently delete cancelled tickets before their applicable retention period expires.

### B. Tenant Deletion Reversal
- Allow reversal only during the 30-day deletion grace period.
- Require a formal reversal request from an authorized Tenant Admin or explicitly authorized requester.
- Require approval from two different, independent authorized Platform Admins.
- The requester cannot approve their own reversal request.
- Both approvals must be independently recorded and audit logged.
- Reversal must be completed before permanent data purge begins.
- Once irreversible deletion or permanent purge has started, normal reversal is prohibited.
- Following approved reversal, cancel the pending deletion and restore the tenant through a controlled reactivation workflow.
- Preserve all existing tenant business data, including tickets, customers, users, knowledge documents, conversations, and historical audit records.
- Revalidate tenant configuration, user permissions, authentication, integrations, and background processing before restoring access.
- Record the reversal request, both approvals, timestamps, actors, and final outcome in the audit trail.

These conditions must remain consistent with the previously selected retention, tenant lifecycle, RBAC, and audit requirements.
